papers.title: ReelCache: An Efficient KV Cache Compression and Management System for Multi-Round Video Generation
papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models produce large KV caches during multi-round video generation. Keeping all these KV chunks would consume substantial memory, while rebuilding discarded caches would significantly delay video chunk generation. This paper presents ReelCache, a KV cache compression system for efficient multi-round, long video generation. ReelCache combines an intra-chunk compressor with an inter-chunk cache manager. The compressor applies low-rank decomposition across channels and video coding to the resulting coefficients, predicting the decomposition rank per transformer layer online to meet retained-energy targets. The cache manager shares basis directions across consecutive chunks and organizes chunk states in a tree, allowing generation branches to share historical state while supporting restoration for resume, rewind, and fork. Experiments across five video generation models show that ReelCache reduces KV storage by 14.46-21.13x relative to baselines and accelerates next-chunk generation by 1.25-3.36x, with less than 1% drop in six representative VBench metrics. GitHub: https://github.com/Tianyu9748/ReelCache

papers.title: Extending DBLog-Based Incremental Snapshots to Handle Orphan Rows in CDC Pipelines
papers.abstract: Applications use heterogeneous datastores where a source feeds sinks such as search indexes or data warehouses via change data capture (CDC). As transaction logs have limited retention, CDC alone cannot bootstrap sinks, and traditional approaches either stall source writes or hold back log events. DBLog-based incremental snapshots, adopted by Debezium and Flink CDC, read tables in chunks interleaved with the log without blocking writes or long log stalls and resume where they stopped. After the initial bootstrap, a sink can drift when losing change events or receiving unintended writes. Even a repeated bootstrap can leave orphan rows that exist in the sink and not at the source. A common remedy is to populate a new empty sink, but repairing an existing sink avoids parallel pipelines, a switch and serving traffic from a drifted sink until the new sink is ready. In DBLog's original design, each chunk only emits the latest state of the rows the table still contains, so it does not handle orphan rows. We extend DBLog to delete them using what a chunk read already knows, namely the keys that the range select did not return, emitting a new kind of event that sinks apply as deletes. We also add a repair request that an external process calls with orphan candidates, which the connector checks with its own read, emitting these events for keys confirmed absent. This enables three modes. In the fully integrated mode, every chunk pass removes the orphans it finds during full or periodic repairs. In the second mode, an external drift process hands suspected orphans to the connector. The third mode combines both and is what we recommend. Together, they turn DBLog into a complete data synchronization engine whether a sink catches up on live changes or missing rows, holds wrong column values, or contains orphan rows. Their safety and convergence are formally verified in Isabelle/HOL and Lean 4.

papers.title: A Per-Step Load-Balancing Engine for Expert-Parallel MoE Serving
papers.abstract: In expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts serving, a layer finishes only when the most loaded GPU of its group does. Token routing shifts at every decode step and concentrates on a few experts, so most of the group's reserved GPU time waits on stragglers. Recovering that time means re-deciding, at every layer of every decode step, how each replicated expert's tokens divide between its copies. The exact linear-program solvers that make this decision optimally take longer than many of the layers they serve, and their working set outgrows GPU shared memory at deployment scale. We introduce Relief, a bidirectional pairwise relaxation that makes the linear program unnecessary, coming within a fraction of a point of the per-step optimum in a few passes of integer halving over the token counts. We build and measure three deployments, CUDA kernels on the serving GPU, the same verified engine on an FPGA over PCIe, and a fixed-function block beside the accelerator. On decode routing from three open MoE families, Relief holds the balance near the per-step optimum at every group size and layer time measured. Scored as effective utilization relative to that optimum, the kernel alone matches or exceeds every deployable scheme at every group size, from the hundred-microsecond layer on. The on-die engine widens that lead at every point, recovering up to 37.3 percentage points over the deployed static placement, while adding 0.02% of a current accelerator's transistors.

papers.title: Transactional Data Change for Real-Time Analytics in Lakehouses
papers.abstract: Real-time data analytics has become a key demand for lakehouses. It requires propagating data changes from the data source to the lakehouse in real time, while ensuring ACID guarantees and minimizing resource consumption and impact on analytical query performance. This is highly challenging for a data system according to the RUM conjecture, especially given the read-optimized immutable file storage layer in lakehouses. Existing lakehouses offer only git-style catalog version control on a single table, and they trade data freshness, query performance, and/or resource efficiency to achieve a barely acceptable data-change throughput. In this paper, we propose a novel data synchronization framework, Retina, that enables real-time, cost-efficient, query-performant, and fully transactional data changes in lakehouses. We implement and open-source Retina. Evaluations show that Retina delivers 10-millisecond-level data freshness and over 3.2 million row/s linear-scalable data-change throughput with low resource consumption and query-performance overhead, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art lakehouse systems and lake-compatible HTAP databases.

papers.title: Lessons Not Learned: Why Cross-Chain Bridges Keep Losing Billions the Same Way
papers.abstract: Bridge hacks have cost billions, often without exploiting a code bug. In the cross-chain bridge hacks we catalogue from 2021 to 2026, failures of security posture, meaning how a bridge's people, code, controls and off-chain infrastructure are set up, account for 88% of reported losses since 2023, and nearly all repeat earlier failures. Code audits cannot catch these failures, so we propose a bridge security assessment rubric. It scores each bridge deployment from on-chain evidence, and a hard cap drops the score to the lowest value when a fatal risk is present. A token is only as safe as its weakest deployment if all its deployments share one backing. For attacks nobody anticipated, we show that rate limits and an emergency stop still bound the loss. We build an analyzer that applies the rubric to deployed bridges and monitors them for changes, and an agentic analyzer that runs the same checks on any bridge. Operators learn what to fix, and users can compare bridges. Our rubric's controls cut bridge hack losses 105-fold, from \$3.52B to \$33M.

papers.title: PACE: Keeping the Right Tokens in the KV Cache Is Not Enough for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate sessions of up to millions of tokens, far more key-value (KV) cache than one GPU holds, so serving systems keep a small budget of tokens and evict the rest. Eviction methods differ in which tokens they keep but share one goal: that the tokens a later step needs are still cached. We show this is not enough. In 100K-token coding sessions on Qwen3-8B with a 2,048-token budget, a planner-guided policy that keeps over 99% of the needed tokens resident still fails late steps increasingly often: its accuracy falls from 93% to 64% as the gap between a definition and its use grows from 2K to 90K tokens, at residency 0.996. The needed tokens are resident but unretrievable: what grows is their rotary-position distance to the query. We present PACE (Planner-Aware Context Engine), a KV-cache engine that couples plan-aware retention, in which the agent's planner tells the cache which context future steps will read, with bounded positions, which renumber kept tokens so their rotary distance to the query stays below 8K at any session length. In a pre-registered evaluation on fresh tasks, PACE passes 97% of hidden unit tests at 100K tokens, against 42% for H2O and 3% for SnapKV under the same budget, and needs both components: either alone reaches 63% (the combination beats each, p < 10^-4). The result holds with length: in 1M- and 2M-token sessions on one 24 GB GPU, with definitions written 0.9M and 1.8M tokens before use, PACE passes 99% and 100% of checks and recalls every session fact, while bounded positions without foresight falls from 33% to 13%; PACE holds under 0.7 GB of KV state where the full cache would need 147-295 GB. Renumbering is exact, costs no measurable perplexity, and adds 9% wall time. On Mistral-7B, whose coding ability caps it at 40% even with nothing evicted, PACE stays at that ceiling while retention alone falls below it.

papers.title: FirstSwap: Pre-Consensus Trade Approvals for Decentralized Market Design
papers.abstract: Decentralized exchanges typically give traders no execution guarantee until a block is finalized. In the meantime, external prices move, traders strategically delay submission, and block producers can influence inclusion and ordering. We introduce FirstSwap, a DEX built on a constant-function market maker pricing curve that gives traders an early pre-approval before consensus, guaranteeing inclusion and execution within their submitted price limit, with final ordering determined by limit prices rather than by a block producer. We demonstrate the benefits of trade pre-approvals in an economic model combining auction theory with CEX-DEX arbitrage. When the CEX price changes gradually, FirstSwap rewards earlier traders with better prices, discouraging strategic delay and yielding higher social welfare and gains to AMM liquidity providers than a batch auction. When the CEX price jumps abruptly, FirstSwap yields higher welfare and smaller AMM losses than fair ordering. The central challenge is delivering fast trade pre-approvals without consensus. We introduce a decentralized, scaled admissibility protocol under which each validator reserves only a fraction of the available liquidity at every price. A trader obtains approval in a single round of messages with a quorum of validators. Somewhat surprisingly, despite Byzantine validators who may approve trades arbitrarily, we show that all quorum-certified trades are jointly admissible and execute within their limits. Our protocol extends naturally to a setting where buy and sell orders can be pre-approved against each other before a block is finalized.

papers.title: Reproducible LoRA Inference Through Deterministic Split-K Reduction
papers.abstract: Reproducibility is important for LoRA-adapted language models used in repeated evaluation, auditing, and decision-making. However, Split-K kernels used to introduce parallelism in low-rank LoRA multiplications can have the unintended consequence of numerical nondeterminism when partial results are combined using floating-point atomic additions. We investigate this non-determinism in vLLM across GSM8K mathematical reasoning, MBPP code generation, and Jev-style structured toxicity decisions on Civil Comments and introduce a deterministic Triton Split-K implementation. Under identical-input replay, Atomic Split-K=8 produces different FP32 shrink outputs in 97.61% of comparisons, while our Deterministic Split-K=8 shows no observed variation. Repeated atomic inference changes generated outputs in 17.30% of GSM8K and 14.96% of MBPP comparisons, sometimes altering task correctness. Structured-decision probabilities vary in 81.47% of atomic comparisons, with decision flips. Controlled tracing demonstrates how shrink-output differences propagate into the KV cache and how accumulated cache differences can change token decisions and final answers. Our deterministic Triton Split-K=8 implementation preserves parallelism, achieving 16.8-21.1% latency-based speedup over unsplit reduction with only 1.02-2.62% additional latency relative to Atomic Split-K=8.

papers.title: EmbodiedIntentBench: Benchmarking Intent-Driven Runtime Adaptation for Mobile Robotic Missions
papers.abstract: Mobile robotic sensing systems must adapt to operator requirements, limited resources, changing connectivity, and observation opportunities shaped by physical motion. Evaluating runtime strategies therefore requires assessing whether their decisions fulfill mission objectives, beyond isolated perception accuracy or execution efficiency. We present EmbodiedIntentBench, a benchmark for intent-driven runtime adaptation in mobile robotic missions. It represents mission intent through structured contracts for coverage, temporal evidence, reporting, urgency, and resources, and couples simulated unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) workloads with causal, resource-accounted execution. Computation decisions affect mission time, resource use, and which observations can contribute evidence. We evaluate fixed and adaptive perception strategies in multi-phase missions and under changing urgency, connectivity, and battery conditions. In the multi-phase Depot study, a configuration with 87.5% full-bank target recall across visible target observations completes only 1 of 16 missions, whereas a lower-recall configuration completes 14. In an ablation, ignoring execution-induced observation loss increases aggregate mission success and reverses the ordering of two runtime strategies. Replays using Jetson AGX Orin CPU and GPU profiles change the relative success of local and remote strategies. In selected Jetson GPU-profile replays, intent-driven adaptation reduces modeled task energy by up to 28% with unchanged mission success. EmbodiedIntentBench provides an extensible framework for evaluating runtime decisions against mission fulfillment under physical and resource constraints.

papers.title: Edge Computing for Computer Vision in IoT: Feasibility and Directions
papers.abstract: The convergence of decentralized architectures integrating Machine Learning, Computer Vision and Low Power Wide Area Networks is increasingly becoming an integral part of our daily existence. Internet of Things serves as a real-time data conduit enhancing decision making via embedded technology and continuous data exchange. This paper explores the feasibility of Edge Computing as a foundational pillar in this evolving landscape. We experiment under real world, dynamic conditions, evaluate the technological aspects, strategies, process flows and key observations under the broad Edge Computing domain. Research pathways include Multi-access Edge topologies in future 6G networks, model quantization, and satellite-enhanced communication platforms. Additionally, a discussion is added supporting the advanced AI functionalities, including zero-shot learning, multi modal perception, and decentralized generative AI, thereby broadening the scope of intelligent applications across various domains. The significance and research objective of this study are threefold: (1) evaluation of LoRaWAN and satellite IoT communication strategies, (2) analysis of CV workloads on edge hardware and (3) future research directions where Edge Computing can support low-latency, energy-efficient and socially impactful IoT applications. By explicitly addressing these aspects, we aim to establish a clear link between the technological feasibility, ultimately with a practical and socioeconomic relevance.

papers.title: FRESCO: A Novel Consistency Control for Asynchronous Pipeline Parallel Training
papers.abstract: Asynchronous pipeline parallelism can accelerate distributed model training, but suffers from instability caused by inconsistent gradient computations. We identify a fundamental source of this inconsistency: error signals are coupled to forward-time features, not just parameter states. This means that parameters may evolve as long as they preserve forward-equivalence. Leveraging this insight, we introduce FRESCO, which frames asynchronous updates as a constrained optimization problem: it finds the minimal update modification that acts trivially on the activation subspace. We demonstrate that FRESCO consistently outperforms representative asynchronous baselines in LLM pre-training, with the gains most pronounced under deep pipelines and high inconsistency levels: at pipeline depth 32, it reaches the same loss as the strongest baseline with 43% fewer iterations and 30% less wall-clock time, while requiring 8~921$\times$ less memory overhead. Moving beyond the current limitations, FRESCO establishes a new foundation for high-utilization pipeline parallel training, providing a scalable path for large-model development on diverse, resource-constrained systems.

papers.title: Multi-Node Transformers for Object Detection and Captioning Across Distributed Edge Networks
papers.abstract: This paper presents a unified transformer-based framework for object detection and dense region captioning across distributed edge networks. The architecture uses a shared visual encoder followed by detection, region extraction, and autoregressive language-decoding stages, allowing localization and region description to reuse the same image features. This design removes the second image-encoding path required by decoupled detection and captioning pipelines. To support execution on resource-limited devices, a workload-allocation formulation assigns model stages and input streams across connected edge nodes while accounting for execution time, memory capacity, processor utilization, power limits, and intermediate tensor transfer cost. The framework is evaluated on a six-device edge testbed comprising four NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and Orin NX inference nodes and two Raspberry Pi 5 auxiliary CPU nodes, with TensorRT FP16 and INT8 execution on the NVIDIA devices. On a Jetson Orin Nano, the unified INT8 model achieves 38.1 FPS with 3.5 GB peak memory use and 11.8 W measured power. Under four concurrent streams, the proposed allocation achieves 35.2 FPS and 28.4 ms mean end-to-end latency with an internode transfer rate of 6.8 MB/s.

papers.title: MOMENT-DP: Momentum Aware Evaluation of Correlated Noise for Differentially Private Training
papers.abstract: Temporally correlated noise can substantially improve the utility of differentially private optimization, yet candidate mechanisms are commonly designed or evaluated using only partial information about the optimization process, such as workload structure, learning-rate schedules, or local curvature. We study whether persistent optimizer state provides additional information that can change the relative utility of privacy-valid correlated-noise mechanisms. We introduce MOMENT-DP, an optimizer-state-aware framework that models how temporally correlated privacy noise propagates through momentum-based optimization. For locally quadratic objectives, MOMENT-DP expresses privacy-induced final loss through an optimizer transfer operator that jointly captures curvature, learning-rate scheduling, momentum, and temporal noise covariance. NoiseCurve's curvature-aware quadratic criterion is recovered exactly as the zero-momentum, constant-learning-rate special case. Changing only momentum while holding curvature, schedule, privacy calibration, and candidate mechanisms fixed induces genuine mechanism-ranking reversals. The effect persists outside exact quadratic dynamics in per-example-clipped private logistic regression, while remaining unresolved in the neural regime we study. These results establish optimizer state as an under-modeled, decision-relevant axis in evaluating temporally correlated privacy noise.

papers.title: Late but Valuable: Why Deadlines Change the Measured Value of LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly plan and run experiments in automated laboratories. These experiments keep running while the model reasons and run on schedules with hard deadlines. If an LLM-generated answer arrives late, the system executes a safe fallback action instead, such as rejecting a sample. This creates a systems problem that standard serving metrics do not capture. An answer that matches the fallback adds no value, and answers that differ from the fallback may require more reasoning time. Reporting answer quality and latency separately can therefore overstate the value of reasoning. We test this on synthetic sample decisions, where the best choice is known exactly and a runtime enforces the deadline. We compare one LLM's fast mode, which answers directly, with its thinking mode, which reasons first. In a prespecified replay of 1,200 new decisions, thinking answers that missed a deadline were worth about five times as much as on-time ones. Multiplying the on-time rate by the mean answer value predicted about twice the value that thinking delivered. This prediction overstated thinking's advantage over fast mode by 0.0241 per decision, and by 0.0191 in a repeat on 300 new decisions. Both 95% confidence intervals excluded zero. In a single-GPU Qwen3-8B experiment using simultaneous request bursts, raising the number of requests from 8 to 56 reduced the share of thinking answers that met a 45 s deadline from 79.2% to 1.4%, although total output tripled. Evaluations of LLM agents for laboratories should therefore measure each answer's value and arrival time together and score the action that actually runs.

papers.title: RecoGEM: A Serving System for Production-Scale Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) is moving industrial recommender systems (RecSys) from scoring candidate items to autoregressively generating item identifiers. This shift promises higher recommendation quality, but makes serving substantially harder: each request executes a short sequence of dependent decoding steps that explore a large item space and select promising candidates on the latency-critical path. GR not only creates structural mismatches with conventional RecSys pipelines, but also challenges the architectural and optimization assumptions of LLM serving stacks, making direct adoption of existing systems difficult. We present RecoGEM, our production GR serving system. RecoGEM uses a runtime--engine decoupling architecture to move GR-specific serving responsibilities, such as candidate-state transitions and live artifact updates, to a dedicated runtime. Its execution engine exploits GR's short token sequences, large candidate populations, and predictable step shapes to optimize self-attention, candidate selection, and execution planning. RecoGEM has been deployed for over nine months across our production lines, serving applications with hundreds of millions of users and supporting more than ten GR model families. On our OneModel production workloads, RecoGEM reaches over 1,000 QPS per serving instance with P99 latency below 35 ms and a 2.88$\times$ throughput improvement over representative baselines.

papers.title: Mitigating SM-Level Load Imbalance in 3D Gaussian Splatting on GPUs
papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic, real-time rendering on commodity GPUs and is increasingly adopted in generative world models and autonomous driving simulators. However, existing optimizations rely on algorithmic changes that often require retraining, or on specialized accelerators that lack flexibility across evolving 3DGS variants. In this paper, we identify a fundamental inefficiency in GPU-based 3DGS rendering: severe SM-level load imbalance caused by uneven workloads across screen tiles. This imbalance creates a long execution tail, leaving most SMs idle while a few process computationally intensive tiles, particularly in large-scale urban scenes. To address this, we present a software-defined GPU scheduling approach that mitigates the execution tail. Our approach uses a persistent kernel to schedule heavy tiles first and selectively chunks outlier tiles across multiple CTAs. A lightweight per-frame policy determines when and how much to chunk using tile statistics already available in the rendering pipeline. Our approach requires neither retraining nor specialized hardware and can be applied orthogonally to existing optimizations across diverse 3DGS variants. Averaged per scene, it accelerates alpha blending by up to 2.93x on a large-scale urban scene, and by up to 5.6x on its most imbalanced frames, while retaining the original alpha blending formulation.

papers.title: Flash-Fusion: Fast, Expressive Queries over Sensor Streams with LLMs
papers.abstract: Pervasive sensor deployments have generated significant interest in IoT data analysis across fields such as healthcare, transportation and urban planning. At the same time, the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a new tool for exploring IoT data through their expressive, natural language interface. Unfortunately, natural language querying of IoT sensor streams is impractical today: raw telemetry exhausts LLM context windows in fractions of a second at scale, incurs prohibitive per-token costs, and produces hallucinated responses. Existing systems work around these limits with lossy text summarization or unconstrained code synthesis, producing expensive, unverified computations. Multi-step queries compound this problem: logical errors in intermediate operations can derail the final answer. We present Flash-Fusion, an agentic framework for natural-language querying of tabular IoT data. Flash-Fusion identifies which available data fields and supported derivations can answer the user's query, constructs a plan using typed, domain-specific operators, and validates its structure and schema compatibility before executing. Because constructing plans still requires costly LLM reasoning, Flash-Fusion caches validated operator sequences for reuse across compatible queries. A smaller LLM adapts a cached plan's parameters to each query, cutting latency and cost. We evaluate Flash-Fusion across human activity recognition, ECG monitoring, and vehicular telematics, covering direct lookups, multi-step reasoning, predictive tasks, and out-of-scope requests. Flash-Fusion achieves 92.2% query accuracy versus 76.1% for ReAct, the strongest baseline, while completing queries 7x faster and consuming 5x fewer tokens. Flash-Fusion enables users across disciplines to explore IoT data without manually constructing queries.

papers.title: Parallel-in-Time Training of Recurrent Neural Networks for Dynamical Systems Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Reconstructing nonlinear dynamical systems (DS) from data (DSR) is a fundamental challenge in science and engineering, but it inherently relies on sequential models. Recent breakthroughs for sequential models have produced algorithms that parallelize computation along sequence length $T$, achieving logarithmic time complexity, $\mathcal{O}(\log T)$. Since sequence lengths have been practically limited due to the linear runtime complexity $\mathcal{O}(T)$ of classical backpropagation through time, this opens new avenues for DSR. This paper studies two prominent classes of parallel-in-time algorithms for this task, both of which leverage parallel associative scans as their core computational primitive. The first class comprises models with linear yet non-autonomous dynamics and a nonlinear readout, such as modern State Space Models (SSMs), while the second consists of general nonlinear models which can be parallelized using the DEER framework. We find that the linear training-time recurrence of the first class of models imposes limitations that often hinder learning of accurate nonlinear dynamics. To address this, we augment DEER with Generalized Teacher Forcing (GTF), a novel variant within the more general nonlinear framework that ensures stable and effective learning of nonlinear dynamics across arbitrary sequence lengths. Using GTF-DEER, we investigate the benefits of training on extremely long sequences ($T$ approaching $10^5$) for DSR. Our results show that access to such long trajectories significantly improves DSR if the data features long time scales. This work establishes GTF-DEER as a robust tool for data-driven discovery and underscores the largely untapped potential of long-sequence learning in modeling complex DS.

papers.title: PithTrain: A Compact and Agent-Native MoE Training System
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has become the dominant architecture for frontier language models. To meet this demand, production frameworks have built optimized MoE training stacks over years of engineering effort. Yet evolving these stacks for new architectures and system optimizations remains expensive. With the rise of AI coding agents, they could automate parts of training-framework development and accelerate this evolution. But applying them to these existing frameworks carries hidden costs, invisible to today's throughput-only evaluations. We name this missing dimension agent-task efficiency (ATE): the cost of using coding agents to understand, operate, and extend a framework. Grounded in four agent-native design principles, we build PithTrain, a compact, agent-native MoE training framework supporting pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. We further introduce ATE-Bench, covering real-world training-framework tasks. Our evaluation shows PithTrain achieves throughput competitive with production frameworks and higher agent-task efficiency on ATE-Bench. On new-feature tasks, PithTrain uses up to 62% fewer Agent Turns than Megatron-LM, and up to 44% and 64% less Active GPU Time than Megatron-LM and TorchTitan, respectively.

papers.title: DDBench: A Benchmark for Agentic Debugging on Distributed Systems
papers.abstract: LLM-based coding agents have advanced rapidly on single-process SWE tasks, with frontier models now clustering in the high-70s on SWE-bench Verified. Distributed-system debugging, however, remains an under-explored regime: bugs span processes, nodes, and protocol interactions, with root causes rarely recoverable from source alone and brute-force exploration intractable across non-deterministic interleavings. This leaves two gaps in LLM and agent evaluation: no code-repair benchmark targets distributed-system bugs, and no controlled study isolates how much externally provided debugging context changes agent success on them. We introduce DDBench, a code-repair benchmark of 60 historical bugs mined from 13 open-source distributed systems, partitioned into three reasoning-scope tiers. DDBench evaluates every case under two matched conditions: a symptom-only condition where the agent receives only the bug symptom and repository, and a context-augmented condition where it additionally receives bounded debugging context (logs, traces, runtime state, and targeted code-investigation notes), isolating the effect of debugging context from model capability. The evaluation of 10 LLMs on DDBench reveals several findings. First, distributed debugging exercises a reasoning dimension that single-process benchmarks do not surface: models' pass rates span 45 pp, and pairwise bootstrap separates 6 of 15 top-tier model pairs at p < 0.05 on DDBench's hardest case-set. Second, bounded debugging context lifts aggregate pass rate by +19.0 pp, and the lift is asymmetric: weaker models gain more in pass rate, while stronger models gain more in efficiency. Third, debugging context requires careful curation, as even faithful debugging context can anchor a strong model on the wrong layer of the system when its observation sits far from the fault.

papers.title: CIDERS: Cloud-Edge LLM Collaborative Learning via Accelerating Personalized Bilevel Optimization
papers.abstract: Amid the rapid advancement of physical-world intelligence, cloud-edge collaborative large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising roadmap for practical LLM deployment. However, existing cloud-edge paradigms struggle to balance global consensus with local personalization, which fails to satisfy the need for a unified knowledge foundation on the cloud and domain-specific adaptation at the edge. To address this, we introduce, for the first time, a personalized bilevel optimization framework that formalizes cloud-edge LLM collaboration as a dual structure: the upper level optimizes edge-side personalization, while the lower level governs cloud-side knowledge transfer, reaching cloud-edge evolving in coordination. We then propose CIDERS, an efficient solver that decomposes the model into a learnable backbone and a messenger. While the cloud performs knowledge transfer to the learnable backbone, the key lies in embedding global trajectories into each local personalization step via consensus-variate correction to reconcile personalization with consensus. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis, including a geometric characterization of the local trajectory and a full convergence guarantee, revealing an explicit trade-off structure between personalization and global convergence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CIDERS consistently outperforms competitive baselines on the compressed edge path, with 3.1x and 1.7x gains on mathematical reasoning and code generation, respectively, and a 10\% relative gain on instruction metrics. Mechanism experiments attribute these gains to early consensus-corrected coordination and task-aware distillation. Overall, CIDERS offers a viable path toward consensus-guided continuous personalization in cloud-edge LLM systems.

papers.title: Multi-Turn Semantic Caching for Low-Cost LLM Serving
papers.abstract: Semantic caching lowers the cost of serving large language models (LLMs) by reusing stored responses for similar requests. In multi-turn conversations, whether a cached response is acceptable depends on both conversations' histories, which embedding similarity of requests and histories predicts poorly (AUC 0.62--0.74 on five workloads). We therefore learn the \emph{reuse risk}, the probability that a cached response is unacceptable, from judge feedback, and choose a budgeted set of conversation states to cache by weighing the generation cost a reuse avoids against a price for unacceptable reuse. We propose CUCB-SC-MT, which learns a cache from logged conversations with a suboptimality guarantee, and CLCB-LS-MT, which learns online and has $\tilde O(\sqrt N)$ regret over $N$ requests when conversation states recur. On math-tutoring (SocraTeach) and movie-ticketing (Taskmaster-3) conversations, both achieve lower loss than prior semantic caching approaches: ContextCache, multi-turn variants of ElastiCache and vCache, and single-turn semantic caching at every cache budget. With 1,000 cache entries, CLCB-LS-MT avoids 35--41\% of the generation cost through acceptable reuses, against at most 22--25\% for the baselines, and lowers estimated serving latency by 19--35\%.

papers.title: Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline for Multi-Instance Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: We present the Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline (ASP), an offline rollout scheduler for multi-instance asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) of large language models (LLMs). ASP jointly reduces three sources of rollout underutilization - padding bubbles from intra-minibatch length heterogeneity, skewness bubbles from long-tail outputs, and sorting bubbles from fluctuations in training-queue occupancy induced by output-length-sorted dispatch - through a single offline preprocessing pass. This enables efficient multi-instance rollout that overcomes the early scaling plateau of single-instance inference while reducing fluctuations in the supply of generated samples to the trainer. We integrate the scheduler into an asynchronous architecture that decouples rollout from training while keeping policy lag observable and bounded. Within our asynchronous architecture, ASP's scheduling reduces mean iteration time by 10.9%. The complete system improves end-to-end throughput by up to 3.22 times and reduces iteration time by up to 76.8% relative to MindSpeed-RL, while reducing iteration time by up to 62.5% relative to verl. It also scales more robustly with additional generation resources than these baselines and shows no visible convergence degradation in the measured bounded-lag regime. ASP has since been used in an internal telecom-domain RL post-training workflow, reducing the reported training period from more than three months to two months and producing a domain-enhanced model for knowledge answering and tool calling.

papers.title: HeteroTask: Multi-Variant Task Scheduling and Execution on Distributed Heterogeneous Clusters
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous systems that combine CPUs and GPUs across multiple servers offer substantial compute capability but complicate scheduling. For DAG-based applications with multiple task implementations, effective execution requires coordinating variant selection, device placement, and data movement. Offline planning can exploit global dependency information, yet plans derived from isolated kernel profiles may diverge from execution because of runtime overheads. We introduce HeteroTask, a framework integrating kernel-wise profiling, PEFT-based multi-variant planning, host-buffer lifetime modeling, and schedule-driven MPI execution. A Bayesian-optimization loop calibrates empirical overhead corrections for repeated, fixed-DAG workflows on exclusively allocated nodes. We evaluate five benchmark and workflow-derived applications on up to six 8-GPU nodes. On two 8-GPU nodes, HeteroTask reduces application-level completion time by 19.7-72.1% relative to the compared StarPU implementations. For Canny Edge Detection, calibration reduces task-window makespan by 25.0% relative to planning without overhead corrections. Combined with CPU/GPU variant selection, calibration reduces it by 58.9% relative to an uncalibrated GPU-only execution.

papers.title: Continual Instruction Tuning for LLM-ased Management of Continuum Resources
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for resource management across the Cloud-Edge continuum. However, embedding LLMs directly inside latency-sensitive control loops places inference latency, execution jitter, and hallucination risks on the critical path. This study argues for a different use of LLMs: a continually instruction-tuned intent compiler that runs once per management intent or declared context change, above a fast, deterministic tactical controller that handles all low-latency runtime actions. We formulate intent compilation as a continual instruction tuning problem, because management intents arrive sequentially and accumulate while infrastructure and workload contexts drift. Unlike recent LLM-based management frameworks, our design scores the model's outputs by execution, so that catastrophic forgetting can be measured in the executed objective of the underlying controller. On a continuum simulator with a 2B backbone and parameter-efficient adapters, preliminary results show that naive sequential tuning forgets earlier intents in the executed objective, that replay of stored examples nearly prevents this forgetting, and that the tuned compact compiler performs on par with simpler translators while being more robust than a grammar parser to rephrased intents.

papers.title: OneReel: Efficient Multi-Scene Video Generation with Scene-Structured Attention
papers.abstract: Multi-scene video generation must follow scene-specific prompts while preserving consistency across scenes. Dense joint generation enables cross-scene information exchange but incurs quadratic attention cost, whereas separate generation avoids this cost at the expense of cross-scene consistency. We present OneReel, a training-free system that exploits scene structure to enable efficient multi-scene generation. Our key insight is that multi-scene generation can preserve complete intra-scene attention while restricting cross-scene information exchange to a bounded shared memory. OneReel uses scene prompts and durations to establish scene-specific attention scopes and dynamically selects a bounded set of representative latent frames for cross-scene sharing. This reduces video attention complexity from quadratic to linear in the number of scenes. To translate these savings into execution speedups, OneReel packs scene-local and shared K/V into dense variable-length attention and employs work-balanced multi-GPU partitioning with communication-aware selection between K/V gathering and Ulysses-style parallelism. Our evaluations across four video generation models show that OneReel achieves 1.7-4.9x end-to-end speedup over dense attention and 1.2-2.2x over existing sparse-attention advances, while improving text-following accuracy by 34-37 percentage points and maintaining cross-scene consistency.

papers.title: Performance Benchmarking of Federated Learning Frameworks for Medical Image Classification
papers.abstract: Selecting a Federated Learning (FL) framework requires understanding the resource demands of its training and evaluation workflow. This work compares Flower, NVIDIA FLARE, and FedBioMed using two-dimensional MedNIST classification with ResNet-10 in a containerized, single-host environment. Following a dated review of repository activity and documented medical applications, we evaluated nine configurations per framework, with three random seeds, for a total of 81 executions. The configurations varied federation size, communication rounds, and batch size. We monitored execution time, CPU and RAM consumption, host-level GPU utilization, server network traffic rates, and model accuracy at the end of each execution. The implementations shared nominal learning settings while retaining differences in data splitting and federated evaluation. Configuration-blocked non-parametric analysis identified differences in execution time, client and server memory, GPU utilization, and network traffic rates. NVIDIA FLARE exhibited the lowest server-memory consumption and the highest host-level GPU utilization, Flower exhibited the highest average server network traffic rate, and FedBioMed required more client memory and longer execution time. No statistically significant difference in final accuracy was detected within the evaluated short training schedules; this does not establish convergence or equivalent predictive performance. The results characterize the configured workflows under shared hardware resources. They provide a concrete case study of system behavior, with conclusions bounded by workflow asymmetries, local networking, and the lightweight MedNIST workload.

papers.title: DICOMPUTE: An Economic and Privacy-Aware Framework for Distributed Artificial Intelligence Inference
papers.abstract: The prevailing design of large-scale artificial intelligence inference concentrates accelerators, model weights, and request processing in centralized computing facilities. Centralization offers important benefits in accelerator utilization, high-bandwidth interconnects, operational control, and serving efficiency. Yet centralized infrastructure is not always the least-cost or most governance-compatible choice for every inference workload. This paper develops a research framework for DICOMPUTE, a heterogeneous distributed inference architecture in which policy-constrained scheduling can allocate suitable requests across privately controlled, regional, and independently operated computing resources. We derive a full-cost comparison that accounts for capital amortization, energy, network transfer, orchestration, utilization, failures, and trust-related expenses; characterize conditions under which distributed inference can outperform centralized alternatives; and specify a privacy model separating data residency, transport confidentiality, execution confidentiality, and verifiable accounting. We propose falsifiable hypotheses and a reproducible experimental design, without presenting simulated examples as measured performance. Our central conclusion is conditional: distributed inference is most promising for divisible, latency-tolerant or locality-sensitive workloads on underutilized compatible hardware, while centralized clusters retain structural advantages for tightly coupled, memory-intensive, high-throughput inference. The framework is intended to support rigorous evaluation rather than to assert universal superiority.

papers.title: Firepool: Brokering Warm GPU Capacity for Agentic and RL Workloads at LinkedIn
papers.abstract: AI agents and reinforcement-learning (RL) trainers run thousands of short, isolated GPU jobs: tool calls, verifiers, and rollouts. A job often finishes in seconds, but starting a GPU pod for it takes 20-35 s even when the container image is already on the node, and minutes when it is not. A warm pod removes the wait only if it can serve the next job, and keeping pods warm must neither waste GPUs nor leak state between callers. Firepool, the sandbox and execution broker behind agentic and RL workloads at LinkedIn, meets both requirements. It makes pods interchangeable by building them from a shared base image per hardware profile and binding each job's code, extra dependencies, and cluster topology when the job starts. It keeps them warm cheaply and safely by reusing a pod only for the caller that used it last, staging zero-VRAM standby pods in fractional GPU shares alongside active pods, and capping the GPUs that warm pools may hold via queue-driven budgets. Over a sampled peak period in production, Firepool serves 94.7% of 3,206 pod requests from warm or standby capacity. In paired benchmarks with fixed-duration jobs on production H200 nodes, agent and RL loops finish 13x and 10.8x faster than with a fresh pod per job; against a fresh reuse tag per job, warm reuse cuts p90 start latency from 59.1 s to 3.5 s. When a job cannot reuse the previous pod, standby promotion shortens the handover wait from 51 s to 0.94 s. In local and simulated runs, a keep-alive matched to the loop's pauses keeps the latency benefit while holding about half the capacity of an always-on pool.

papers.title: Network Contention State Aware Dynamic Optimizer for Accelerator Collective Communication Libraries
authors: MD S Q Zulkar Nine (Arkansas Tech University)
papers.abstract: Collective Communication Libraries (CCL) are critical for large-scale distributed AI/ML training, yet their configurations are determined by static heuristics that do not account for real-time network conditions. Our empirical study shows that these heuristics perform near-optimally in contention-free environments, but degrade substantially under background traffic. To address this, we present a cooperative multi-agent run-time optimizer for accelerator collective communication. Our approach employs a two-agent architecture: (i) detector- a Long Short Term Memory(LSTM) recurring neural network fed classifier head with a sequential probability ratio test that distinguishes sustained contention from transient spikes; and (ii) selector- a configuration selector built on a Dueling Double DQN (D3QN) with Conservative Q-Learning that adapts configuration parameters in response. We implemented this dynamic tuner over NCCL, a widely used CCL developed by NVIDIA. When evaluated on Chameleon Cloud's isolated bare-metal cluster, this dynamic tuning approach reduces AllReduce latency by 36% over NCCL and 32% over a fully converged AutoCCL. We further evaluated it across six real AI workloads spanning convolutional networks, transformers, and recommendation architectures. Our multi-agent tuner approach delivers up to 65% speedups on Delta cluster with NVIDIA A100 GPUs and Slingshot-11 fabric internode connectivity.
